18.01.title: Measurement uncertainty
18.01.html:
A measurement without an uncertainty is only half a result. “The flow is 7.3 L/s” says little. “7.3 L/s, 95 % interval 3.5 to 12.1 L/s” tells the reader whether the number can support a decision. The international rulebook is the GUM, the Guide to the expression of uncertainty in measurement (JCGM 100:2008).

Standard uncertainty: type A and type B

Every input xi​ gets a standard uncertainty u(xi​), the standard deviation of what you believe about it. The GUM names two ways to get it:

  • Type A, from statistics of repeated readings. For n readings with sample standard deviation s, the uncertainty of the mean is u=s/n​.
  • Type B, from anything else: a resolution, a calibration certificate, a tolerance. If all you know is that the value lies within ±a, a rectangular distribution gives u=a/3​.

Both kinds are then treated the same way. The labels say how you got the number, not how much you trust it.

Propagation by linearisation

For a result y=f(x1​,…,xN​) with independent inputs, a first-order Taylor expansion gives the combined standard uncertainty

uc2​(y)=i=1∑N​ci2​u2(xi​),ci​=∂xi​∂f​.

The ci​ are sensitivity coefficients, and each term ci2​u2(xi​)/uc2​ is that input’s share of the uncertainty budget. For a power law y=x1a​x2b​, this reduces to relative uncertainties: (uc​/y)2=a2(u1​/x1​)2+b2(u2​/x2​)2. The expanded uncertainty U=kuc​ with k=2 gives roughly a 95 % interval when the result is close to normal.

Propagation by Monte Carlo

GUM Supplement 1 skips the Taylor series. Draw M samples of every input from its distribution, push each set through f, and read the mean, the standard deviation and the 2.5 % and 97.5 % percentiles of the results. It costs a few hundred thousand function calls and needs no derivatives. When f is close to linear over ±2u of its inputs, both methods agree. When it is not, Monte Carlo is the one to believe.

Worked exampleg from a pendulum, then a weir that breaks linearisation

Pendulum. Ten stopwatch readings of 20 swings: 40.13, 40.21, 40.08, 40.17, 40.25, 40.11, 40.19, 40.06, 40.22, 40.15 s. The length to the bob centre is L=1.000 m ±2 mm (tape measure).

  1. Period T=2.00785 s. Type A: u=0.00099 s. Add the 0.01 s stopwatch resolution as type B, 0.01/3​/20, to get u(T)=0.00103 s.
  2. u(L)=0.002/3​=0.00115 m.
  3. g=4π2L/T2=9.7926 m/s². Sensitivities: ∂g/∂L=9.7926 s⁻², ∂g/∂T=−2g/T=−9.7543 m/s³.
  4. uc​=0.0151 m/s², so g=9.793±0.030 m/s² (k=2). The budget is 56 % length and 44 % period: a better tape measure helps as much as more timing.
  5. Monte Carlo with 400 000 samples: mean 9.7926, u=0.0151, 95 % interval [9.7639, 9.8214]. The methods agree to better than 1 %. The local value in Zurich, 9.807 m/s², is inside the interval.

Weir. Q=32​Cd​b2g​h1.5 with Cd​=0.62±0.02, b=0.50 m ±5 mm, and a small head h=40±8 mm (ripples on the staff gauge).

  1. Linearised: Q=7.323 L/s, U=4.420 L/s, interval [2.903, 11.744] L/s.
  2. Monte Carlo: mean 7.434 L/s and 95 % interval [3.465, 12.088] L/s. Because h1.5 is convex, the mean is biased 1.5 % upwards and the interval reaches 4.77 L/s above the estimate but only 3.86 L/s below it. Linearisation cannot see either effect. Report the Monte Carlo interval, and if the decision matters, measure the head in a stilling well.

Exercise 1The budget of a density measurement

A steel cylinder has mass m=245.3±0.1 g, diameter d=25.00±0.02 mm and length L=64.00±0.05 mm (all standard uncertainties). Find ρ=4m/(πd2L), its relative uncertainty and the biggest term in the budget.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. ρ=4×0.2453/(π×0.0252×0.064)=7808 kg/m³.
  2. Power law with exponents 1, −2, −1: (u/ρ)2=(0.1/245.3)2+(2×0.02/25)2+(0.05/64)2.
  3. Terms: (4.08×10−4)2, (1.60×10−3)2, (7.81×10−4)2. Sum 3.34×10−6, so u/ρ=0.183 %, u=14 kg/m³.
  4. The diameter dominates (77 % of the budget) because it enters squared. Measure it at several positions and use a better micrometer.

18.02.title: Sensors and transducers
18.02.html:
A transducer turns the quantity you care about into one you can measure, usually a voltage. A thermocouple turns temperature into microvolts, a piezo crystal turns force into charge, and a strain gauge turns stretch into a tiny change of resistance. This lesson takes the strain gauge apart, because the same bridge circuit sits inside load cells, pressure sensors and torque meters.

The strain gauge

A foil gauge is a zig-zag of thin metal on a plastic backing, glued to the part. Stretch it by strain ε and its resistance changes:

RΔR​=GFε,

with the gauge factor GF≈2 for constantan foil. At 1000 µε (a steel part at about 200 MPa) a 350 Ω gauge changes by only 0.74 Ω. You cannot read that with an ohmmeter while it drifts with temperature, so you put the gauge in a bridge.

The Wheatstone bridge

Four arms R1​,R2​,R3​,R4​ form two voltage dividers across the excitation V. The output is the difference of the two mid-points:

Vout​=V(R1​+R2​R1​​−R3​+R4​R4​​).

With all four equal the bridge is balanced and Vout​=0, whatever V is. Write Ri​=R(1+xi​) with small xi​ and expand to first order:

Vout​≈4V​(x1​−x2​+x3​−x4​).

Opposite arms add and adjacent arms subtract. That one line explains every bridge configuration:

  • Quarter bridge: one active gauge, x1​=GFε. Exactly, Vout​=Vx/(4+2x), so Vout​≈VGFε/4 with a non-linearity of about x/2.
  • Half bridge on a bending beam: gauges on top (+ε) and bottom (−ε) in adjacent arms. Vout​=VGFε/2 exactly, twice the signal.
  • Full bridge: four active gauges, Vout​=VGFε.

Temperature makes every gauge on the part read the same apparent strain. In adjacent arms it cancels, so a half bridge, or a quarter bridge with an unstrained dummy gauge in the adjacent arm, is temperature-compensated.

Worked exampleA 350 Ω gauge at 1000 µε

GF=2.1, V=5 V, so x=GFε=0.0021.

  1. Quarter bridge. Exact Vout​=5×0.0021/(4+0.0042)=2.62225 mV. The linear formula gives 2.62500 mV, a non-linearity of 0.105 %. It grows to 0.52 % at 5000 µε and 1.04 % at 10 000 µε.
  2. Half bridge: 5.25000 mV, full bridge: 10.50000 mV, with no non-linearity at all.
  3. Temperature. Warm the part by 10 K with 1.5 µε/K of apparent strain. The quarter bridge drifts by 39.4 µV, which looks like 15 µε of load. With a dummy gauge or in a half bridge the drift is zero.
  4. Lead wires. 10 m of 0.14 mm² copper each way adds RL​=2.50 Ω in series with the gauge. That desensitises the quarter bridge by RL​/(R+RL​)=0.71 %. A three-wire connection puts one lead in each adjacent arm and cancels most of it.

Exercise 1Size the amplifier

A full bridge with GF=2.0, V=10 V carries ±500 µε at full load. You want ±2.5 V into an ADC. What gain do you need, and what is the bridge output per µε?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Full bridge: Vout​=VGFε=10×2.0×500×10−6=10 mV at full load.
  2. Gain =2.5/0.010=250.
  3. Sensitivity 10×2.0×10−6=20 µV per µε before the amplifier, 5 mV per µε after it.

18.03.title: Sampling and aliasing
18.03.html:
A data logger does not record a signal. It records a list of numbers, one every Ts​=1/fs​ seconds. Between the samples it knows nothing, and that ignorance has a precise and dangerous consequence: two different signals can produce the same samples.

Why sines can impersonate each other

Sample x(t)=sin(2πft) at tn​=n/fs​. Replace f by f+kfs​ for any integer k:

sin(2π(f+kfs​)n/fs​)=sin(2πfn/fs​+2πkn)=sin(2πfn/fs​).

The samples are identical. Also sin(2π(fs​−f)n/fs​)=−sin(2πfn/fs​), the same sine with a sign flip. So every frequency folds into the band 0≤f≤fs​/2, and a component at f shows up at the alias

fa​=​f−fs​round(fs​f​)​.

The Nyquist-Shannon theorem

If the signal contains nothing at or above fs​/2 (the Nyquist frequency), the samples determine it completely, and sinc interpolation rebuilds it exactly. If it does contain energy above fs​/2, no processing after the fact can tell it from a real low-frequency component. Hence the rule of every data-acquisition system: put an analogue anti-aliasing filter in front of the ADC, and sample several times faster than the highest frequency you care about.

The wagon-wheel effect

A film camera samples a moving picture. A wheel with N identical spokes looks the same every 1/N of a turn, so the picture repeats at the spoke frequency Nfrot​. If that is above half the frame rate it aliases. The eye follows the nearest spoke, and the wheel appears to turn at

fapp​=NNfrot​−fs​round(Nfrot​/fs​)​,

which can be slow, zero or negative.

Worked exampleA vibration logger and a car on film

Logger. A 200 Hz logger with a 1024-point FFT and a Hann window. The code builds the FFT from scratch and checks it against np.fft.fft.

True frequency, Hz FFT peak, Hz Alias formula, Hz
30 29.998 30
110 89.997 90
180 20.002 20
230 29.998 30
397 3.003 3

A 180 Hz gear-mesh vibration reads as a convincing 20 Hz peak. Nothing in the data says it is fake.

Car. A 6-spoke rim, tyre diameter 0.63 m, at 50 km/h, filmed at 25 frames per second.

  1. frot​=(50/3.6)/(π×0.63)=7.0174 rev/s. Spoke frequency 6×7.0174=42.104 Hz, above the 12.5 Hz Nyquist limit.
  2. 42.104−25×2=−7.896 Hz, divided by 6 spokes: the wheel seems to turn backwards at 1.3159 rev/s. Tracking the nearest spoke frame by frame in the code gives the same number.
  3. It looks frozen whenever Nfrot​ is a multiple of 25 Hz: at 29.69 km/h and 59.38 km/h.

Exercise 1Choose a sampling rate

A pump runs at 1450 rpm with 7 impeller vanes. You want to see the blade-pass frequency and its second harmonic without aliasing. What is the minimum sampling rate, and what would a 250 Hz logger show instead of the blade-pass tone?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Shaft 1450/60=24.17 Hz. Blade-pass 7×24.17=169.2 Hz, second harmonic 338.3 Hz.
  2. Nyquist needs fs​>2×338.3=676.7 Hz. In practice use 1 kHz or more with an anti-aliasing filter at about 400 Hz.
  3. At 250 Hz: ∣169.2−250∣=80.8 Hz. The logger shows an 80.8 Hz tone that does not exist.

18.04.title: Filters
18.04.html:
Real sensor signals carry noise: mains hum at 50 Hz, vibration from a motor, electronic hiss. A low-pass filter keeps the slow part you care about and removes the fast part. In code a filter is a difference equation, a few multiplications per sample, and the whole design job is choosing its coefficients.

The RC filter

A resistor in series with a capacitor, output across the capacitor:

RCy˙​+y=x⟹H(s)=1+sRC1​,∣H(jω)∣=1+(ωRC)2​1​.

The cutoff fc​=1/(2πRC) is where ∣H∣=1/2​ (−3 dB). Above it the gain falls by 20 dB per decade. That is gentle: a tone at 5fc​ is only reduced to 0.196.

Butterworth: as flat as possible

The n-th order Butterworth filter has ∣H(jω)∣2=1/(1+(ω/ωc​)2n), maximally flat in the passband and falling by 20n dB per decade. For n=2:

H(s)=s2+2​ωc​s+ωc2​ωc2​​.

From s to a difference equation: the bilinear transform

Sampling at fs​ with period T, replace s by

s=T2​z+1z−1​,

where z−1 means “one sample ago”. This maps the stable left half-plane exactly into the unit circle, so a stable analogue filter stays stable. It also squeezes the infinite analogue frequency axis into 0≤f<fs​/2: an analogue frequency ωa​ lands at ωa​=(2/T)tan(ωd​T/2). Pre-warping sets K=tan(πfc​/fs​) so the cutoff lands where you asked. For the second-order Butterworth:

yn​=b0​xn​+b1​xn−1​+b2​xn−2​−a1​yn−1​−a2​yn−2​,
b0​=b2​=a0′​K2​,b1​=2b0​,a1​=a0′​2(K2−1)​,a2​=a0′​1−2​K+K2​,a0′​=1+2​K+K2.

The resulting digital magnitude is exactly 1/1+(tan(πf/fs​)/K)4​, slightly better than the analogue prototype near Nyquist.

Worked exampleClean an accelerometer signal

fs​=500 Hz, fc​=10 Hz, second-order Butterworth.

  1. K=tan(π⋅10/500)=0.062915. Coefficients: b0​=b2​=0.00362168, b1​=0.00724336, a1​=−1.82269493, a2​=0.83718165. Both poles have ∣z∣=0.914976<1, so the filter is stable.
  2. Gains: 0.999205 at 2 Hz, 0.707107 at 10 Hz, and 0.037467 (−28.53 dB) at 50 Hz. The analogue prototype gives 0.039968 at 50 Hz: the bilinear warping helps here.
  3. Running the difference equation on 10 s of the noisy signal, a least-squares fit of the output tones gives gains 0.9992 at 2 Hz and 0.0374 at 50 Hz, matching ∣H∣.
  4. The price is phase lag: 16.40° at 2 Hz, a 22.77 ms delay. For a controller that delay matters (lesson 18.13). For offline analysis, running the filter forwards and then backwards cancels the phase.
  5. A first-order RC with the same cutoff only reduces the 50 Hz tone to 0.1901.
  6. With SciPy installed, the coefficients match scipy.signal.butter(2, 10, fs=500) and the output matches scipy.signal.lfilter to rounding error.

Exercise 1An RC filter in hardware

You want a 100 Hz RC low-pass in front of an ADC with a 10 kΩ resistor. What capacitor do you need, and how much does the filter attenuate a 1 kHz component?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. C=1/(2πRfc​)=1/(2π×104×100)=159 nF. Use the standard 150 nF, giving fc​=106 Hz.
  2. At 1 kHz with fc​=100 Hz: ∣H∣=1/1+102​=0.0995, about −20 dB.
  3. One decade above the cutoff gives only a factor of 10. If 1 kHz noise must not alias, use a higher-order filter or a faster ADC.
